articles.title: Trump's media bans 'deprive the public', press freedom groups argue
articles.summary: The plaintiffs allege they are no longer able to do their work without reliable access to information delivered by the White House press.
articles.body:
Press freedom groups are suing the Trump administration over its efforts to block mainstream US news outlets from covering the White House, according to court filings.

The six plaintiffs, which include scholars, advocates and journalists, argue media bans issued by the White House violate the First Amendment of the US Constitution - a critical statute that provides broad protections for the press and freedom of speech.

Their suit comes after CNN, Politico, and MSNOW brought a separate legal challenge over the White House's attempts to revoke or restrict their press access.

The Knight First Amendment Institute and Yale Law School's Media and Information Access Clinic filed the legal case on the plaintiffs' behalf.

The six plaintiffs have asked a New York federal court to declare the White House's selective media bans violate the First Amendment, and to block the administration from continuing to enforce it.

In court filings, the plaintiffs allege they are no longer able to do their work without access to information delivered by the White House press.

The White House policy, they claim, "deprives the public" of reporting, and forces journalists who cover Donald Trump "to account for the possibility that a critical or ill-advised word about the president may result in their access being summarily restricted or revoked".

Such a ban has a "distorting effect" on coverage from the White House, the court filing argues.

The BBC has asked the White House for comment.

The lawsuit did not ask a judge to award financial damages, only to require the defendants to cover their legal fees if they win.

Since Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, the White House has engaged in a contentious standoff with many longstanding US media outlets, which the president has frequently accused of publishing "fake news".

Last month, it banned reporters from CNN, Politico, and MSNOW from the White House, leading several other media organisations to temporarily suspend their pooled coverage of the president in protest.

The affected news outlets sued, arguing the White House was illegally discriminating against them because of the content of their coverage.

A federal judge later ordered the White House to restore the credentials of the impacted journalists while their lawsuit plays out.

The reporters later said they were allowed back into the White House complex.

Major US outlets suspend shared Trump coverage in protest at media ban

What is the White House pool and why is it in a row with Trump?

Media outlets banned by Trump resume White House coverage after judge's order

The White House has, however, continued to selectively bar journalists, which news organisations in the US argue violates their press freedom protections.

CNN, for instance, has threatened to take further legal action in court as its reporters continue to be denied access aboard Air Force One to cover the president.

And last week, the White House banned a correspondent from The Independent from covering the president's trip to the state of Iowa, after Trump berated the reporter from the UK news outlet during a press conference.

In his second term, Trump has also moved to bring conservative bloggers, influencers and other "new media" figures into the press room, arguing it is necessary to provide diverse perspectives in White House coverage.

In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool - the small group of journalists that has access to the president on any given day - which for more than a century had been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.

The same month, the White House moved to bar Associated Press journalists from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because the outlet used the term "Gulf of Mexico" rather than "Gulf of America".

AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

Trump last week confirmed he is considering moving the entire press corps from the White House grounds following reports he was contemplating the reconstruction of a swimming pool that sits underneath the James S Brady briefing room.

"I am thinking about moving the press, and putting them in a different location," he wrote on Truth Social. "I will use that location for very badly needed space."

articles.title: Man charged with sending white substance to 4 lawmakers
articles.summary: An Illinois man is facing federal charges related to mailing letters containing a white substance to four members of Congress this month in an act inspired by reports of suspicious packages being sent to dozens of lawmakers and election officials across the country. Matthew Unglesbee, 37, is charged with one count of false information and…
articles.body:
An Illinois man is facing federal charges related to mailing letters containing a white substance to four members of Congress this month in an act inspired by reports of suspicious packages being sent to dozens of lawmakers and election officials across the country.

Matthew Unglesbee, 37, is charged with one count of false information and hoaxes and one count of mailing threatening communications, according to a criminal complaint unsealed Monday. He made an initial appearance in federal court via video Monday afternoon.

An accompanying affidavit states that FBI personnel responded to three congressional members’ offices in the Northern District of Illinois last Wednesday after receiving an anonymous tip.

Letters containing a “white granular substance” — later determined to be salt — were found along with handwritten notes that read “HA HA,” according to the affidavit. A fourth envelope was also found at a U.S. senator’s office with the message: “HAH enjoy the gift.”

The envelopes identified Unglesbee as the sender and included his home address, the FBI said.

Court documents indicate that Unglesbee told FBI agents Sunday that he sent the letters. He claimed that he was “joking” but knew it could be perceived as a threat.

The document states he said he chose salt because it “kind of looks like” anthrax, which he knew recipients took seriously and would have “hazmat come in white suits.”

A fifth unmailed, empty envelope addressed to a congressional office in D.C. was also found during a search of Unglesbee’s home, according to the documents.

Dozens of congressional offices from both parties have reported receiving mail containing an unknown white powder in recent weeks, prompting a federal investigation. Unglesbee has denied any involvement in those other incidents.

articles.title: Trump says Brazil’s election results ‘looked rigged’
articles.summary: President Trump dismissed Brazil’s presidential election results as “rigged” Monday after the South American country’s liberal President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection. “It looked terrible to me,” Trump said when asked if he thought Sunday’s election was fair. “I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election, frankly,” the president said.…
articles.body:
President Trump dismissed Brazil’s presidential election results as “rigged” Monday after the South American country’s liberal President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection .

“It looked terrible to me,” Trump said when asked if he thought Sunday’s election was fair.

“I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election, frankly,” the president said. “It was a terrible look for the world.”

“Elections have to be indisputable, and it looked very bad to me,” he added.

The incumbent Brazilian president, commonly known as Lula, defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, who is the son of Brazil’s former far-right leader Jair Bolsonaro, in Sunday’s runoff election. The elder Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after he lost the 2022 presidential election to Lula.

While Trump did not formally endorse the younger Bolsonaro, he endorsed his father in 2022. Lula has also been an outspoken critic of Trump, and his win in South America is seen as a victory for the political left, which has experienced a string of defeats on the continent in recent years.

Trump and Lula have exchanged a number of barbs over the years.

Last year, Trump imposed a 50 percent tariff on Brazil in part over the prosecution of the elder Bolsonaro. Lula hit back at Trump in an opinion piece from The New York Times in September, calling the president’s tariffs “illogical” and misguided.

The two presidents met face to face in the White House last May, while the younger Bolsonaro met with Trump later that month.

articles.body:
MS NOW’s Joe Scarborough on Monday slammed negative reactions to former President Obama’s recent joke about the Cheesecake Factory and the White House.

“Can you believe how stupid the reaction is and how stupid they think Americans are?” he said on his show, “Morning Joe.”

“Every time Donald Trump opens his mouth now, especially in this end run, they say such unbelievably stupid things that suggest that they think all Americans are dumb,” he added.

On Saturday, Obama made fun of President Trump’s multiple renovation projects in Washington while at a campaign stop in Cleveland.

“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of Trump’s White House construction efforts.

“What’s with the gold? … He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” the former president quipped.

Obama added that he thought Trump was more focused on renovating the White House than on issues voters cared about.

Some Republican figures did not react positively toward the Cheesecake Factory comparison.

Conservative pundit Scott Jennings went after the former president in a post on the social platform X, saying Obama “makes speeches for 500k a pop.”

“Hasn’t eaten dinner that costs less than $250 in years. Has never been in a Cheesecake Factory. Undefeated at condescending to regular folks. Will always be known for a presidency that ushered in the Trump era to begin with,” Jennings said in his Saturday post .

A representative for the Cheesecake Factory did not return The Hill’s request for comment on Obama’s comments.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: James Comey charged for a third time by the Trump administration
articles.summary: The former FBI director, a longtime target of President Donald Trump, hasn’t been indicted in the latest case.
articles.body: Federal prosecutors have charged former FBI Director James Comey with transmission of national defense information and conspiracy to transmit national defense information. It’s the third federal case against Comey, who has been a longtime target of President Donald Trump since he initiated the FBI investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. The case has played out under seal since Oct. 5. Comey’s defense attorneys filed a motion 10 days ago to dismiss the charges. He has not been indicted in the case. Comey responded to the new charges in a video Monday. “Well, they’re back again. It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to,” Comey said in a video on Substack after the charges were made public. “Nothing’s changed with me. I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary,” he said. The new charges stem from an Oct. 5, 2016, article in The New York Times with the headline “Yahoo Said to Have Aided U.S. Email Surveillance by Adapting Spam Filter” by reporter Charlie Savage. “The United States’ investigation has uncovered evidence that former FBI Director, James B. Comey, sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before,” Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Dustin Farahnak wrote in a filing unsealed Monday. “The investigation has uncovered evidence that Mr. Comey directed staff to speak to Mr. Savage about specific accuracy concerns related to the Reuters article, and thereby illegally transferred classified information.” Comey’s attorneys argued that both counts “are based exclusively on the October 5, 2016, alleged disclosure exactly ten years before the government’s filed criminal information” — and that the charges should be tossed out because of statute-of-limitations issues. The case is “time barred,” they argue, because the government had 10 years to bring the case “by obtaining a grand jury indictment.” The charges that were filed are a criminal information — essentially a charge filed by prosecutors, not a grand jury indictment — and should therefore be dismissed, they argue. Comey cannot be tried on the criminal information alone unless he waives indictment, which would be an unusual move. Prosecutors will still need to seek an indictment, if the court permits it, before Comey can be arrested on the charges, arraigned, enter a plea and ultimately be tried. The case was unsealed by U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden, who noted that the facts underlying the investigation “have been subject to considerable press coverage.” McFadden said that while it is not unusual to “initially seal a charging instrument,” those are usually sealed only to aid the apprehension of a defendant. Prosecutors maintain that the charges are timely and that Comey’s attorneys are misreading the applicable law. A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement that its filing was meant to “toll,” or pause, the statute of limitations. “Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further,” the spokesperson said. Comey was the FBI director when the Times article was published. Trump fired him in May 2017 after he launched an investigation into Russian election interference in the 2016 presidential race and potential ties to the Trump campaign. Trump has repeatedly called for Comey to be prosecuted in the years since, calling him a “dirty cop” and a “sick person.” The criminal case is the third to be brought against Comey since Trump’s second term began. The first case was dismissed by a judge; the other came on April 28, when Comey was indicted in North Carolina on charges he made a threat against Trump when he posted an image of seashells arranged to read “8647.” Comey has maintained his innocence. Comey attorney Patrick Fitzgerald said in a statement Monday that the first case was dismissed after “the Department of Justice used a person who was not actually a United States Attorney to seek an Indictment that was not actually shown to the grand jury. And it charged Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit. That case was promptly and properly dismissed.” “In April 2026, the Department of Justice filed charges in the Eastern District of North Carolina concerning Mr. Comey’s posting of a photograph of seashells spelling ‘8647.’ We will not comment beyond our filings in that case,” he added. Fitzgerald said the most recent case involves an article “that two different teams of prosecutors investigated during the first Trump administration. Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an ‘Information’ against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury” and “purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit.” “Mr. Comey will fight these charges vigorously and in the open,” he said. The unsealing of the charges comes the same day that a federal judge ruled that Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, had been unlawfully fired from the Justice Department last year and ordered that she be reinstated.

articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent mocked former President Obama outside a Cheesecake Factory in Washington on Monday after Obama likened recent White House renovations to the famous restaurant chain during a Saturday rally.

“Well, two things. This is the man who built the museum that looks like Darth Vader’s tomb,” Bessent said while exiting a Cheesecake Factory location near the White House, according to a clip from Fox Business. “I would tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try.”

The comment refers to Obama’s home on the Massachusetts island , which the family has visited frequently since leaving the White House in 2017. The home sits on nearly 30 acres fronting the Edgartown Great Pond. Bessent, for his part, has bought and sold more than $127 million worth of U.S. real estate, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024.

The Treasury secretary added that he has always gotten the French dip cheeseburger from the Cheesecake Factory, and it was “excellent” Monday.

Obama on Saturday blasted President Trump during a campaign stop in Ohio, saying the president “seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV.”

“What’s with the gold? … He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” the former president quipped, referring to the late Iraqi authoritarian leader.

He also criticized Trump’s other renovation projects around Washington, including the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, noting that “some no-bid contract got it all messed up.”

The Washington Post reported the Trump administration is expected to spend at least $900 million on White House construction projects.

Obama was in Ohio to campaign for Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), who’s hoping to take back his seat in the upper chamber. Acton and Brown are attempting to navigate a midterm environment that has proved tumultuous for the GOP amid Trump’s approval rating hitting a historic low.

When asked about the Republican Party’s chances in the fast-approaching midterm elections, Bessent responded, “I’ve been out on the campaign trail with the president, and there’s great enthusiasm.”

A New York Times/Siena poll, using the generic ballot, found 51 percent of respondents said they were likely to vote for the Democratic candidate for Congress, while 39 percent chose the Republican candidate.

The midterm environment has also affected GOP Senate candidates who are facing tough Democratic challengers in red strongholds like Texas and Kansas.

articles.body:
AI safety group calls on White House to support AI chips security bill

The AI safety advocacy group Americans for Responsible Innovation (ARI) is urging President Trump to endorse the Chip Security Act, stating the president’s support would “send a clear message” to America’s competitors.

The letter, shared exclusively with The Hill on Monday, argues the Chip Security Act would help the federal government detect when U.S.-made chips are diverted to adversaries.

The bill, first introduced by Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) in May 2025, would direct the Commerce Department to require a “location verification mechanism” on AI chips subject to export controls.

Chip exporters would then be required to report to the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) if their products were diverted from the intended destination or tampered with.

ARI stressed that the bill would also have the Commerce Department evaluate the other safeguards needed to prevent theft or tampering of chips.

“Your endorsement of the Chip Security Act would send a clear message to America’s competitors like China, and adversaries like Russia and Iran looking to acquire some of America’s most powerful technologies: the United States will defend its technological edge and go after any illicit access to the advanced chips that power it,” ARI President and former Rep. Brad Carson (D-Ariz.) wrote in the letter, dated Monday.

The White House has yet to take a stance publicly on the bill and did not respond to The Hill for comment by publication time.

Numerous reports over the past two years have indicated AI chips from U.S. companies like Nvidia were smuggled to China despite Washington’s export controls.

During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington last month, he and Trump discussed AI , agreeing to launch new talks on the subject. They also agreed to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents, and the first AI-specific talk is scheduled for November.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent proposed an AI safety notification system for Trump and Xi to consider during talks. Carson said ARI supports this system.

articles.summary: Presented by Alliance for Aging Research {beacon} Health Care Health Care The Big Story Poll shows broad support for reinstating enhanced ACA subsidies With the midterm elections almost a week away, a new poll shows broad support across the political spectrum for reinstating the enhanced Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies that congressional Republicans allowed to…
articles.body:
Poll shows broad support for reinstating enhanced ACA subsidies

With the midterm elections almost a week away, a new poll shows broad support across the political spectrum for reinstating the enhanced Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies that congressional Republicans allowed to expire.

According to the survey from Florida-based pollster Inquire shared first with The Hill, 76 percent of respondents said they support restoring the enhanced subsidies, including 60 percent of Republicans.

Most GOP members of Congress opposed extending enhanced ACA subsidies last year, with many citing fraud.

Democrats shut down the government for a record 45 days last year but failed to get an extension of the enhanced credits in return for their support on voting to reopen the government.

Instead, Republicans promised to give them a vote on a bill of their choosing to extend the subsidies. The vote failed, and the subsidies expired at the start of this year.

As a result, health insurance expenses for thousands of ACA enrollees spiked . Most people remained eligible for some subsidies, but primarily middle-class enrollees who earned too much for base-level subsidies were shut out.

The poll is yet another warning sign for Republicans who worry that the high cost of healthcare is one of the party’s greatest liabilities. In key battleground states, Democrats are hammering their opponents for voting to cut Medicaid and for allowing the enhanced subsidies to expire, driving up premium costs.

According to the poll, 57 percent of voters said they are more likely to back a congressional candidate who supports extending the credits , and 56 percent said they are less likely to back one who let them expire.

Democrats are campaigning on restoring the subsidies as one of the first priorities they will tackle should they win control of either chamber of Congress , though it will be an uphill fight with President Trump in the White House regardless.

Voters also said they blame Republicans over Democrats for letting the enhanced subsidies expire, by a 53 percent to 26 percent margin. While a majority of Republicans blamed Democrats, 19 percent blamed their own party .

The survey of 1,023 people was conducted from Oct. 17-21, with a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points.

articles.title: DOJ charges Comey for third time
articles.summary: Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged again by the Justice Department (DOJ) for allegedly disclosing sensitive national defense information in 2016, according to newly unsealed court documents. Comey was charged with two counts of transmitting information and conspiring to transmit information related to national defense matters on Oct. 5, but a federal judge…
articles.body:
Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged again by the Justice Department (DOJ) for allegedly disclosing sensitive national defense information in 2016, according to newly unsealed court documents .

Comey was charged with two counts of transmitting information and conspiring to transmit information related to national defense matters on Oct. 5, but a federal judge granted his request to unseal the complaint Monday.

The DOJ alleges that Comey “through one and more co-conspirators” directed an individual to share classified information with a reporter from a national news organization in October 2016, according to the charging document. The publication is identified in other court documents as The New York Times.

A separate unsealed DOJ filing cited an Oct. 5, 2016, article by Times reporter Charlie Savage that contained information “significantly similar” to talking points that had been circulated in an internal government email hours before it was published.

“The United States’ investigation has uncovered evidence that former FBI Director, James B. Comey, sought to correct information which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before,” DOJ attorneys wrote. “The investigation has uncovered evidence that Mr. Comey directed staff to speak to Mr. Savage about specific accuracy concerns related to the Reuters article, and thereby illegally transferred classified information.”

Comey denied any wrongdoing in a video posted to his Substack account on Monday afternoon, blasting the prosecution as an “appalling abuse of the Department of Justice.”

“Nothing’s changed with me,” he said. “I’m still innocent but I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent judiciary.”

Comey has moved to dismiss the case. His lawyers noted in court filings that the disclosure had been previously investigated by two separate U.S. attorney’s offices, both of whom declined to bring charges.

They also argued that the charges should be thrown out because the 10-year statute of limitations for certain espionage-related offenses “explicitly demands” an indictment, which has not been secured in Comey’s case.

The government brought the charges by a “criminal information,” which does not require a grand jury.

“This Court should enforce the text that Congress wrote and dismiss the information as time barred,” Comey’s lawyers wrote.

This is the third time that the Justice Department has pursued charges against Comey as part of what critics see as a push to target and prosecute President Trump’s perceived political foes.

Comey is already facing federal charges in North Carolina in connection with a now deleted social media post of seashells arranged to read “86 47,” which the Justice Department has claimed was a threat to Trump’s life.

A first attempt to prosecute Comey for allegedly lying in 2020 congressional testimony collapsed after a federal judge found the U.S. attorney handpicked to the pursue the charges, Lindsey Halligan, had been unlawfully appointed.

articles.title: Trump offers $1 million reward for voter fraud tips that lead to convictions
articles.summary: It’s unclear where the money would come from for Trump’s latest effort to crack down on purported voter fraud ahead of the midterm elections.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Monday that he is offering $1 million to anyone who reports voter fraud in the upcoming election or past ones. Trump did not specify where the funds for such payments would come from. He said on Truth Social that they would be paid on the “arrest and conviction of those that created the fraud.” A White House spokesperson did not offer more details about the offer, referring NBC News to Trump’s post. There is no evidence of widespread voter fraud in U.S. elections, though Trump has spent years claiming that there is and that it cost him the 2020 election he lost. Instances of voter fraud do occur on occasion — such as when people fill out recently deceased relatives’ ballots or lie on mail ballot applications — and they are usually caught. A tracker from the conservative Heritage Foundation has collected more than 1,600 incidents of voter fraud over 40 years, a tiny fraction of the total votes cast over that period. Trump’s offer Monday is his latest effort to exert greater influence over the midterm elections. His administration has dedicated significant resources to searching for noncitizens on states’ voter rolls. The Justice Department sued California officials in an attempt to force them to segregate mail ballots it says went to potential noncitizens. Noncitizen voting is also rare, studies show. Last week, the Justice Department sued Alaska officials, at Trump’s request, to prevent the results of the U.S. Senate race from being certified if GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. Courts have also blocked Trump from making sweeping changes to mail voting and requiring documentary proof of citizenship to vote. Trump’s voter fraud reward announcement comes after he unveiled a $25 million government fraud whistleblower program, telling reporters he’d decide who was worthy of the prize. He has also been making other financial promises as he hits the campaign trail for Republicans ahead of the midterms, including $5,000 payments to Americans if his party maintains control of Congress. Trump has similarly not clarified where the money for those payments would come from.

articles.title: The Memo: El-Sayed allies argue Trump’s anti-Muslim attacks will backfire
articles.summary: President Trump is intensifying his anti-Muslim attacks on Abdul El-Sayed in the final stretch of campaigning before Election Day. At a Sunday rally in Michigan, Trump unleashed a volley of Islamophobic comments against El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee who is seeking to become the first Muslim senator in history. Trump said El-Sayed is “on the side…
articles.body:
President Trump is intensifying his anti-Muslim attacks on Abdul El-Sayed in the final stretch of campaigning before Election Day.

At a Sunday rally in Michigan, Trump unleashed a volley of Islamophobic comments against El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee who is seeking to become the first Muslim senator in history.

Trump said El-Sayed is “on the side of the terrorists” and alleged that if he and the Democrats prevail in the election “they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadis to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror.”

The president also insinuated that El-Sayed’s worldview was similar to the 9/11 hijackers and said that he should “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”

The appeal to anti-Muslim prejudice is a world away even from the emotionally fraught days right after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Then-President George W. Bush visited the Islamic Center of Washington, D.C., six days after those attacks, emphasizing the positive contributions of Muslim Americans to U.S. life and saying, “The face of terror is not the true faith of Islam. That’s not what Islam is all about. Islam is peace.”

A quarter-century later, it would be impossible to imagine Trump expressing such sentiments.

He has referred numerous times to El-Sayed as a “jihadist” and has also invoked the candidate’s middle name, Mohamed, in a mocking way akin to his references to former President Obama’s full name, Barack Hussein Obama.

Trump has dismissed criticism of such tactics, saying last week, “I’m the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want.”

El-Sayed has largely sought to shrug off the attacks.

“I’ll be Senator Mohamed to you, bro,” he said Sunday during a rally on the other side of Michigan.

Obama, campaigning alongside El-Sayed and other Democratic candidates, also drew the parallel to his rhetorical battles with Trump in the past.

“We have seen this movie before,” Obama said Saturday in Detroit. “I starred in it. I have a long form birth certificate to prove it.”

Voices supportive of El-Sayed contend that the viciousness of the Trump attacks is likely to backfire, even if it appeals to some fervent members of the president’s base.

“It’s just a sign of desperation on Trump’s part and the part of the GOP,” said Matt Duss, executive vice president at the Center for International Policy. “We have seen them leaning into those kinds of remarks about Abdul — or attacks on others about ‘communism’ — because they have no achievements to run on. It’s trying to scare their base to the polls.”

It’s plausible that Islamophobic attacks from Trump will drive turnout up to even higher levels than might have been expected in Michigan’s Muslim communities.

Michigan has the highest concentration of Arab Americans in the nation — estimated at between 300,000 and 400,000 people. In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, this dynamic powered some heated debates about the Biden-Harris administration’s policies on Israel and Gaza, likely helping Trump eke out a narrow victory in the state.

Abdelhalim Abdelrahman, the communications director of American Muslims for Palestine and a native of Michigan, called Trump’s most recent attacks on El-Sayed “horrible, disgusting and incendiary.”

“For the longest time, Arab and Muslim Americans have been waiting for a moment like this, where someone with their name and background is ascending to some of the highest levels of the American system. Whenever we endure these kinds of hateful attacks, I think it hardens the resolve of the community.”

El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, has stopped several notches short of Trump’s rhetoric.

Appearing on NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday, Rogers told NBC moderator Kristen Welker, “I’ve never called him a terrorist.”

Rogers did, however, say that El-Sayed had a “relationship with the thinking of the Muslim Brotherhood.”

Rogers made reference to an open letter El-Sayed signed in 2012 in support of then-newly elected Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, who was indeed affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood. The previous year, El-Sayed penned a HuffPost column urging the U.S. to support Egyptian street protests against Morsi’s autocratic, American-backed predecessor, Hosni Mubarak.

However, Morsi was democratically elected. El-Sayed’s HuffPost column was in effect arguing the Brotherhood was more moderate than it is often portrayed.

During the “Meet the Press” interview , Welker also resurfaced a quote from 2012 in which Rogers himself said that there were “moderate Muslim Brotherhood individuals” to whom the U.S. should reach out, though “we are going to have to watch it carefully.”

Rogers contended that Welker was “trying to twist this thing.”

For the moment, El-Sayed seems to have a slight advantage in a close race. The Hill’s data and polling partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) gave the Democrat a 67 percent chance of prevailing as of Monday. DDHQ’s polling average shows El-Sayed leading by a little under 2 points.

Richard Czuba, founder of the Michigan-based Glengariff Group, a nonpartisan research firm, said that Trump’s attacks on El-Sayed could consolidate Democratic support beyond El-Sayed — for reasons beyond the Muslim issue itself.

He drew a parallel with how Trump’s jabs at Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) several years ago strengthened her hand for her 2022 reelection bid.

“We are seeing exactly the same thing about El-Sayed,” Czuba said. “Every time Trump opens his mouth and attacks him, Democrats — who came out of that polarized primary — put aside their concerns and rally to his side.”

El-Sayed defeated Rep. Haley Stevens (D) in a contentious August primary in which views of Israel loomed large.

David Dulio, a professor of political science at Michigan’s Oakland University, noted that, for all the media attention sparked by Trump’s attacks, economic issues still dominate. He said the campaign was “driven by the economy,” including rising gas prices.

“That’s not to say there aren’t folks out there who are being mobilized by those Trump attacks,” Dulio added. “I just think part of the strategy has been to make Abdul El-Sayed unacceptable as a U.S. senator. They have tried multiple tactics, and this is one of those areas of attack.”

Above all, Dulio also sounded a note of caution on predictions of the outcome.

“The state of the race is: It’s close,” he said.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Appeals court rules against DOJ in California ballot fight
articles.summary: A federal appeals court panel Monday refused to order California to set aside 20,000 mail ballots that the Trump administration says are likely from noncitizens. In a 2-1 vote, the panel found it has no jurisdiction and the administration needs to wait for the trial judge to rule. He’s set to hold a hearing Tuesday, but…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court panel Monday refused to order California to set aside 20,000 mail ballots that the Trump administration says are likely from noncitizens.

In a 2-1 vote, the panel found it has no jurisdiction and the administration needs to wait for the trial judge to rule. He’s set to hold a hearing Tuesday, but the Justice Department has demanded faster action since ballots are being returned each day.

“The United States’s claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one,” the court wrote in its unsigned ruling.

The Trump administration sued California earlier this month as the state rebuffed claims that it sent mail ballots to 20,000 likely noncitizens for the midterm contests. The suit seeks to keep the ballots segregated so they can be verified before being counted.

The majority comprised U.S. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, appointed by President Trump, and U.S. Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, appointed by former President Biden.

In dissent, U.S. Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, a Trump appointee, warned the ballots in question may not be able to be identified later.

“The question—does the federal government have the power to stop this potential attack on the integrity of our elections?” Bumatay wrote. “Under both federal law and the Constitution, the answer must be ‘yes.’”

As the Justice Department demanded speed and began racing up the appellate ladder, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit agreed to convene for a rare weekend hearing to consider the case. Its ruling is not a final decision in the litigation, and the Trump administration could now try to ask the full 9th Circuit bench or the Supreme Court for an emergency intervention.

Otherwise, it’s headed back to the trial court Tuesday afternoon for a high-stakes hearing before U.S. District Judge David Carter, an appointee of former President Clinton who has moved the case along but not quite at the speed the administration has demanded.

As the clock ticks closer to next Election Day next week, voters across California have begun returning their ballots. Court documents show that in Los Angeles County alone more than 331,000 mail ballots have been received.

“Fantastic news in our defense against Donald Trump’s attacks on our Constitution and elections,” California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) wrote on X. “Make no mistake: Trump won’t stop trying to illegally seize power or deface our democracy. California will keep fighting back.”

articles.title: Appeals court hands Trump administration setback in push to block California votes by alleged noncitizens
articles.summary: The ruling said the DOJ failed to give a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the California case and therefore it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in.
articles.body: A U.S. appeals court on Monday ruled against President Donald Trump's administration in a major voting dispute ahead of the midterm elections, denying a request to block California from counting mail ballots from people on a list of more than 20,000 registered voters the federal government alleges are likely noncitizens. The 2-1 decision by the San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals marked the latest setback in Trump’s efforts to assert a greater federal role in overseeing elections in the run-up to the Nov. 3 midterms in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. The majority decision said the Justice Department had failed to give a lower court judge an adequate opportunity to consider the case, and therefore it would be premature for the appeals court to weigh in. The lower court judge has scheduled a hearing on Tuesday in the case. Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, one of the two judges in the majority, wrote in a concurring opinion that the federal government “asks the federal court to dictate to a state legislature a matter squarely within the state’s traditional domain, upending the state’s policies in this regard and inviting disorder and confusion for voters and election officials alike.” The lawsuit was an escalation in the Trump administration’s pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting and a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process weeks before an election. The California lawsuit was the first time the Trump administration sought to prevent a state from counting votes, though it did not indicate how many of the 20,000 people on its list had actually submitted a mail ballot. Justice Department officials said Oct. 19 that the 20,000 people included 28 who had been criminally charged with illegally voting. California is the most populous state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state. Democrats are seeking to regain control of the House from Trump’s fellow Republicans in the midterms. Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its “sanctuary state” policies that ‌limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. Trump has long asserted that California’s immigration policies have facilitated voter fraud. All available evidence indicates that ineligible voting, including noncitizen voting, is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation published in July found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally; many appeared to stem from voter confusion or administrative errors, rather than intentional fraud. The Justice Department filed its lawsuit on Oct. 15 in federal court in Los Angeles. The lawsuit asked a federal judge to order California to separate any ballots it received from people on the administration’s list from the rest of the ballots and not to count them until it had verified that the people who cast the ballots were citizens. The Justice Department filed an emergency motion with the 9th Circuit to expedite the case. California says the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and asserted in a court filing that the Justice Department’s assertions relied on “suspect data.” “At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” lawyers for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in a court filing Tuesday. “At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.” Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the Trump administration’s methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizens risk wrongly flagging naturalized U.S. citizens for removal from the rolls. The Justice Department has told election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots. It has sued 30 states and Washington, D.C., for refusing to provide complete voter rolls including voters’ sensitive personal data but has lost 26 of those cases so far without winning one. “Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country’s democracy,” said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat.

articles.title: House GOP to hold leadership elections a week after Election Day
articles.summary: House Republicans are slated to hold their leadership elections on Nov. 10, according to two GOP staffers, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Members also have…
articles.body:
House Republicans are slated to hold their leadership elections on Nov. 10, according to two GOP staffers, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Politico, which first reported the news , noted that Republicans will hold a two-hour candidate forum that morning before voting on the leader, whip, conference chair and other positions.

Members also have until Nov. 6 at noon to declare whether they want to run for a position, according to the outlet. If Republicans retain control of the House, a floor vote for Speaker will take place at the beginning of the next Congress in January.

It remains unclear whether Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) will seek another term as the party’s leader, with Republicans facing the possibility of losing their House majority in the midterms.

Johnson initially floated the idea of returning to Louisiana if Republicans lost the House, in an exclusive interview with Fox News. His spokesperson quickly pushed back on speculation that Johnson would leave Congress.

Johnson later told CBS News that he intends to remain the party’s leader even in the “unlikely scenario” that Republicans lose the House, saying he would “expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government.”

“But what I believe is, I’m going to be the Speaker of the House for at least two more years,” Johnson added.

Decision Desk HQ forecasts that Democrats are favored to win back the lower chamber.

Some GOP lawmakers and aides previously told The Hill that there could be a potential push to support someone else as leader besides Johnson if the party suffers major losses in the midterms.

Some GOP staffers have floated House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (Ohio) as contenders for minority leader if Republicans lose the House.

articles.title: Billionaire with Epstein ties emerges as top Dem donor bankrolling ads weaponizing disgraced financier’s files
articles.summary: Reid Hoffman, who faced scrutiny over Jeffrey Epstein ties, is among the largest donors funding Epstein-themed ads targeting GOP candidates.
articles.body: Reid Hoffman, the billionaire co-founder of LinkedIn who has faced scrutiny over his ties to Jeffrey Epstein, was among the largest donors to House Majority PAC, a key Democratic fundraising group that is now using Epstein-themed ads to target GOP candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings released last week. In recent weeks, HMP has begun spending heavily as Election Day nears, pressing the case that Republicans have failed to make good on promises to bring transparency to Epstein’s child sex trafficking activities and whether he facilitated illegal sexual encounters for others. The filings do not identify which donor funds were used for specific advertisements, but Hoffman’s contribution came as HMP ramped up spending on Epstein- focused ads just two weeks ahead of election night. In one such campaign, HMP targeted Rep. Nick Begich, R-Alaska, over his vote against a procedural motion that would have advanced consideration of the Epstein Files Transparency Act. Begich later voted in favor of the legislation, which passed with near-unanimous support. EPSTEIN-LINKED BILLIONAIRE POURS $500K INTO SUPER PAC BACKING KENTUCKY DEMOCRAT: 'DIRTY EPSTEIN-CLASS MONEY' "How did Jeffrey Epstein hide it? He was protected by the elites — elites like Nick Begich. Begich voted against releasing the Epstein Files, trying to hide the truth. Alaskans need someone who cares more about bringing down costs than protecting a rapist," the ad claims. The legislation, which became law in November 2025, requires the Justice Department to release records related to Epstein, with some protections to conceal the identity of his victims. HMP has spent $543,300 on the ad campaign, according to FEC records. But the group has also targeted races in a number of other battleground states, spending $ 480,000 in Iowa’s Second Congressional District, $ 2.06 million in Pennsylvania’s 1st District, $550,150 in Arizona’s 2nd District and $628,000 in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District. All the ads launched within the past week, according to ADMO, an advertising- tracking service. TRUMP-LINKED SUPER PAC PULLS FUNDING FROM 2 HOUSE REPUBLICANS AS GOP FIGHTS TO KEEP MAJORITY At least one Republican argued that Hoffman’s ties to Epstein made his contribution — and HMP’s Epstein-focused ads — hypocritical. "Democrats have no problem with money in politics so long as it benefits their own campaign, even if it comes from certified perverts like Reid Hoffman who maintained a relationship with Epstein after his conviction," Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Democrats have no morals when power and money are on the line, and they’ll take both from anyone willing to write a check." For many years, Epstein and Hoffman exchanged correspondence and gifts. They also helped raise money for MIT’s Media Lab. According to records made public through the DOJ’s Epstein Files library, Hoffman joined Epstein at his private island and visited him at his residence in New York. In one email, sent on Christmas Eve in 2014, Hoffman told Epstein he had sent him a pair of gifts. "Sent you two gifts to NYC addie. 1 - Ice cream. If you have any interest, you should try — [or] else for the girls. 2 – something that may strike your funny bone for the island," Hoffman wrote, referring to a surfer statue. Hoffman has repeatedly denied wrongdoing, telling The Wall Street Journal in 2019 that he regretted continuing their relationship after Epstein was convicted in 2008 on charges of soliciting prostitution from a minor. "My last interaction with Epstein was in 2015. Still, by agreeing to participate in any fundraising activity where Epstein was present, I helped to repair his reputation and perpetuate injustice," Hoffman said in 2019. "For this, I am deeply regretful." EXCLUSIVE: OSSOFF CHALLENGED TO RETURN EPSTEIN-LINKED DONATION OR RETRACT 'EPSTEIN CLASS ATTACK' There is no allegation in the records cited by Fox News Digital that Hoffman participated in Epstein’s sex-trafficking crimes. articles.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to why removing Ilhan Omar from Congress could be harder than Trump expects
articles.summary: President Trump is urging Rep. Ilhan Omar to resign as the Justice Department investigates potential immigration fraud, raising questions about whether House Republicans could take action against the Minnesota Democrat.
articles.body: Republicans hope there are lots of Democrats who won’t win re-election next week and return to Capitol Hill. Republicans are imploring voters to kick them out. But President Trump is focused on bouncing one Democrat from Congress who likely wins re-election in a solidly blue district. That’s Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.). She carried her district two years ago with nearly three-quarters of the vote. But President Trump questions whether Omar is in the country legally and, therefore, qualified to sit in Congress. "She used a fake name to be sworn in," said the President. "She's a little troublemaker." The Department of Justice is investigating Omar for potential immigration fraud. Federal authorities raided her Washington, DC home recently and removed 17 items. That included phones, notebooks, a camera and a Somali phrase book for her kids. President Trump suggests that her name is not "Ilhan Omar" and that it’s "an entirely different name name. Ihan Nur Sayeed Elmi. It's close." A federal filing in that inquiry lists the Congresswoman’s name as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar." That’s why the President says "she must immediately resign from Congress." A reporter for Fox Digital confronted the Congresswoman about her name. SOMALI RAP PROMISING TO 'SCATTER' ENEMIES UNDERSCORES OMAR'S SERENE LAKESIDE VIDEO "Is your name Ilhan Sayed, Ilhan Nur Sayed Alami, or Ilhan Abdullahi Omar?" asked Rashid Umar Abbasi, working for Fox. "Ilhan Abdullahi Omar. You know it," replied Omar. "Ma'am?" asked Abbasi for clarification. "It's Ilhan Abdullahi Omar," she confirmed. The Clerk of the House of Representatives officially lists the Congresswoman as solely "Ilhan Omar" on 15 different financial disclosure reports dating back to 2018. That’s even before she entered Congress. The same with the Minnesota state legislature where Omar served prior to coming to Washington. The discrepancy is why the President wants the House to banish Omar. "She will not be legally allowed to be a member of that august body that sits in Washington," said President Trump. But it’s not his call. However, Article I, Section 5 of the Constitution grants both bodies of Congress final authority about who it admits to its membership. At least one House Republican is willing to explore that. But only if the facts merit it. "The House has the prerogative to seat or not seat and to throw Members out if it so chooses," said Rep. Morgan Griffith (R-Va.). "There ought to be good sound reasons for it." It’s a different set of rules, but Griffith had experience with this as the Virginia House of Delegates grappled with a similar issue about seating lawmakers in the Commonwealth in 1988. But Congress is altogether different. "It would be extraordinary. And it should be extraordinary and it should not be used except in extraordinary circumstances," said Griffith. Yours truly asked what would meet that bar to block someone from serving in the House. "It's like the Supreme Court said about pornography. I'll know it when I see it," said Griffith, paraphrasing late Justice Potter Stewart from a key 1964 obscenity case. ILHAN OMAR HIT WITH EXPULSION THREAT AS GOP LAWMAKER VOWS TO BOOT HER FROM CONGRESS OVER DOJ PROBE House Republicans have two options to deal with Omar if they are truly determined to take action – regardless of what is proven or not. Qualifications for the House are pretty simple. You must be a citizen and a resident of the state you are representing. And, you must be 25 years old. You could even be convicted of a crime and serving time in jail. The Constitution is silent on all other credentials. You could also have a resume which is without a blemish. It doesn’t matter. The House could still take action against you. The first conceivable option could come now. The Constitution grants the House and Senate the right to expel Members – provided there’s a two-thirds vote. Any scenario to expel Omar seems remarkable. Especially since she hasn’t been convicted of a crime. And even if she is charged, there are lots of other issues which could emerge before a trial. It would be strange to have the executive branch of government trying to remove a Member of the legislative branch of government. Moreover, it’s likely that the House counsel would contest any effort by federal prosecutors to procure Omar’s official House communication devices as well as documents. There’s a firewall between the legislative branch and executive branch known as the "Speech or Debate Clause." Article I, Section 6 of the Constitution grants lawmakers privileges tied to their official duties. So getting those papers — let alone potentially deporting her as some have suggested – is a far cry. Especially since she’s a Member and this all hinges on expulsion. Moreover, two-thirds of the House will never vote to expel a Member under these circumstances unless there’s ironclad proof of wrongdoing. That’s why the House has only expelled six Members in its history. The last was former Rep. George Santos (R-N.Y.) in 2023. However, what may be an issue is whether or not there could be an objection to seating Omar when the new Congress convenes in January. In 1968, then Rep. Adam Clayton Powell (D-NY) faced a criminal investigation. House Speaker John McCormack (D-Mass.) refused to seat Powell – even though he met all other requirements. The Supreme Court ruled in Powell v. McCormack that the House can’t exclude a Member if they meet the basic standards to serve in the House. TRUMP IMMIGRATION WIN COULD STRENGTHEN ADMIN'S HAND IN LOOMING SUPREME COURT FIGHT That said, it’s possible there could be motions not to seat Omar – or even other progressive Members-elect who have said controversial things about the U.S. and Constitution. Such a motion would come right after the House chooses a Speaker. But the Speaker has not sworn-in the rest of the Members. The House would then swear-in everyone – except the Member or Members-elect who may face questions about serving. Once the House swears in the rest of the body, it can then vote on a motion not to expel those persons, table the motion, or refer the motion to a committee for investigation. In 1985, the House did not swear-in Rep. Frank McCloskey (D-Ind.) and decided to investigate whether or not he won his seat in the Hoosier State. The House didn’t swear-in McCloskey for several months. Based on Powell v. McCormack, it’s hard to envision a scenario where the House declines to seat someone. But it might not do it immediately based on the McCloskey case. Of course, it’s always probable that the House could seat someone – and then expel them. That doesn’t collide headlong with the Powell decision. But considering that the House has only expelled six members, those circumstances are doubtful, too. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP What’s in a name? Especially for Ilhan Omar. Her adversaries may raise questions about her name. But it’s doubtful they can do anything about her position.

articles.title: Vance announces $57M grant boost for meatpacking facilities
articles.summary: Vice President Vance announced Monday that the Agriculture Department is investing millions of dollars in new grants toward meatpacking facilities. He made the announcement while campaigning for Sen. Roger Marshall (R) in Kansas. The vice president said the grants would go toward 10 meatpacking facilities in the state, adding that it “could not have happened…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance announced Monday that the Agriculture Department is investing millions of dollars in new grants toward meatpacking facilities.

He made the announcement while campaigning for Sen. Roger Marshall (R) in Kansas. The vice president said the grants would go toward 10 meatpacking facilities in the state, adding that it “could not have happened without Doc Marshall.”

The Agriculture Department in a release said it is investing $57 million to boost ranchers in 40 states to expand their capacity and create “new and better markets through the Meat and Poultry Processing Expansion Program .”

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said the announcement builds on President Trump’s executive order “Promoting Fair Competition in Livestock Markets and Expanding Market Access for American Meat Producers.”

“We are focused on rebuilding the Great American Cattle Herd, and providing more local processing opportunities will continue to give confidence to our ranchers to help us fulfill this goal,” Rollins said in a statement.

The news comes amid a broader series of agricultural announcements made by Trump and Vance as they make rally stops ahead of next week’s midterms.

Last week Vance announced a $1.3 billion investment in domestic fertilizer manufacturing while stumping in Nebraska.

The last time Trump was in Kansas for Marshall he announced an $8 billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program that would give farmers one-time payments to offset the expensive cost of diesel amid the harvest season.

The president also said that if Marshall won, he would push to make the sale of E15 — fuel blended with 15 percent ethanol — year-round, instead of being restricted during the summer months.

Trump also signed an executive order earlier this month that expanded access to tax-exempt, red-dyed diesel . The diesel is dyed red to signal its tax-exempt status but is typically used in farm and construction equipment.

articles.title: Trump fires back at Obama’s Cheesecake Factory jab
articles.summary: President Trump fired back at former President Obama during a Monday night rally in Corinth, Miss., after the former commander in chief likened Trump’s White House renovations to a Cheesecake Factory while on the campaign trail over the weekend. “‘Donald Trump spends a lot of his time fixing up the White House,’” Trump said, mocking…
articles.body:
President Trump fired back at former President Obama during a Monday night rally in Corinth, Miss., after the former commander in chief likened Trump’s White House renovations to a Cheesecake Factory while on the campaign trail over the weekend.

“‘Donald Trump spends a lot of his time fixing up the White House,’” Trump said, mocking Obama. “Isn’t that a nice thing to do?”

“He said, ‘This isn’t a Cheesecake Factory.’ Can you believe it? Which is a very successful company. He doesn’t like successful companies,” the president told supporters in Corinth, going on to tout his renovation projects at the White House.

Obama joked during a campaign stop Saturday in Cleveland that Trump has the White House “looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, it’s just gold everywhere.”

Hussein’s Iraqi palaces were famously adorned with gold fixtures and decor.

“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of the president Saturday.

Trump first lashed out at Obama while speaking with reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland en route to Mississippi.

“He doesn’t understand it because he’s not a smart guy,” Trump said. “The way he ran the country, only a stupid person would run the country like that.”

“We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly. It has to be painted, and the exterior plaster can’t be falling off the walls, and the decorations and the ornaments on the windows that are magnificent can’t be on one side of the window and falling off on the other side,” he continued.

“It’s not about money. It’s about seeing. Guys like Obama don’t see it. He doesn’t see dirt, he doesn’t see filth, he doesn’t see broken ornaments on a building,” Trump said. “For you to say it was a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president.”

articles.title: DHS suspends visa-free travel program for Chinese nationals amid birth tourism, security concerns
articles.summary: The Trump administration suspended visa-free travel for Chinese nationals to the Northern Mariana Islands amid birth tourism and espionage concerns.
articles.body: The Trump administration is suspending a visa-free travel program for Chinese nationals visiting a U.S. island territory after Republican lawmakers warned it could facilitate birth tourism and pose national security risks. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s decision targets a Biden-era program that allowed prescreened Chinese nationals to visit the Northern Mariana Islands for up to 14 days without a visa. In a notice announcing the decision, the Department of Homeland Security cited concerns that the program could facilitate birth tourism, espionage and illegal onward travel to nearby Guam, a key hub for the U.S. military. BIRTH TOURISM FIGHT SHIFTS TO US ‘TROPICAL MATERNITY WARD’ WITH HISTORY OF CHINESE EXPLOITATION The decision comes after senators Mike Lee, R-Utah, Rick Scott, R-Fla., John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Bill Cassidy, R-La., urged Mullin in April to end the program, warning that it encouraged birth tourism and posed national security risks. Lee celebrated the decision in a post on X. BIRTH TOURISM CRACKDOWN EXPANDS AS HOUSE CHAIRMAN RAISES CRIMINAL CONSPIRACY CASE "America is not a nursery for the CCP to steal citizenship," Lee wrote, referring to the Chinese Communist Party. "Thank you, President Trump!" Rep. Chip Roy’s press office also welcomed the move, saying the Texas Republican and Rep. Tom Tiffany, R-Wis., had raised concerns about the program in March. GOP FIREBRAND TARGETS BOOMING BUSINESS LETTING FOREIGNERS EXPLOIT US CITIZENSHIP LAWS "Rep. Roy is pleased to hear the Trump Admin closed this dangerous loophole," his office wrote on X. Birth tourism is when someone travels to the United States primarily to give birth so their child can become an American citizen. Some travelers have hidden the purpose of their trip when applying for a visa. FIRST ON FOX: RUBIO RAMPS UP BIRTH TOURISM CRACKDOWN HOURS BEFORE XI TOUCHES DOWN IN US The program at issue was created in 2024 and took effect the following year. More than 3,000 Chinese nationals used it to enter the Northern Mariana Islands in fiscal year 2025, according to DHS. Those travelers were screened by Customs and Border Protection, but did not have to obtain a visa through a U.S. consulate, the department said. EXCLUSIVE: STATE DEPARTMENT REVOKES OVER 250,000 VISAS IN BROAD IMMIGRATION VETTING CRACKDOWN The suspension is set to take effect at 2 p.m. EDT on Oct. 30 and will apply to both new applicants and travelers who have already been approved. Those already in the territory under the program may finish their authorized stays but will need a visa for future visits unless another lawful exception applies. DHS said the suspension will remain in place while the department evaluates the program with the secretaries of state and the interior. BIRTH TOURISM COULD SOON CARRY A SEVERE NEW CONSEQUENCE FEW WOULD RISK: 'EXISTENTIAL CRISIS' The department warned that the program could make it easier for Chinese nationals to travel to the territory to give birth. "While birth tourism has long been an issue in the CNMI, the availability of visa-exempt travel and reduced vetting under EVS-TAP may lower barriers to this practice," the notice says. HOUSE REPUBLICAN CALLS FOR YANKING STUDENT VISAS OF CHINESE NATIONALS DHS also said birth tourism can strain the islands’ medical system. The notice did not provide a number of births linked to travelers who entered through the program, formally known as the Economic Vitality & Security Travel Authorization Program. The department warned that visa-free travel could be exploited for intelligence gathering near U.S. military facilities. The Northern Mariana Islands are home to Tinian Air Base, while Guam hosts several military installations. TRUMP SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDERS TARGETING BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP, BIRTH TOURISM AFTER SUPREME COURT SETBACK Although the program did not permit visitors to travel to Guam or the U.S. mainland, DHS cited previous cases involving Chinese nationals smuggled by boat from the Northern Mariana Islands to Guam. Those cases involved earlier travel policies or other streamlined arrangements, but DHS said they showed a vulnerability that the newer program had not eliminated. The suspension comes as the Trump administration pursues a broader crackdown on birth tourism. A State Department task force launched Aug. 12 had revoked more than 750 visas tied to suspected birth tourism activity as of late August, the department previously told Fox News Digital. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told Fox News Digital that officials were working with international partners and law enforcement to identify travel patterns that could point to birth tourism networks. Pigott said some networks help visitors conceal the purpose of their trips and then coach them on how to avoid paying medical bills. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Northern Mariana Islands program is separate from the visitor visa process targeted by those revocations. Fox News Digital's Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.

articles.title: White House defends Trump after archbishop calls prayer moment 'manipulated' ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Archbishop Jeffrey Grob accused the White House of manipulating video of an Oval Office prayer with Catholic bishops for political gain before midterms.
articles.body: The White House on Monday defended President Donald Trump after Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob publicly apologized for participating in an Oval Office prayer with the president, accusing the administration of using the religious gathering for political purposes less than two weeks before the midterm elections. Grob issued a statement Sunday titled "A Public Apology," alleging that the White House distributed photographs and video of the Thursday prayer without the consent of the 12 participating bishops. He accused the administration of manipulating a sacred moment. The archbishop said he had received messages from Catholics concerned that the prayer appeared to constitute a political endorsement. Grob acknowledged having reservations before attending and apologized for the distress his participation caused. "I feel a heavy sadness, not only over the pain I caused, but also for the fact that something so sacred to a group of religious leaders, prayer to our Heavenly Father, would be manipulated in that way," he said. "We came in good faith to try to work for the betterment of our fellow human beings, to ease their suffering, to build up the common good, and to pray with a president, not to pose for a political photo opportunity to benefit the few." White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers defended Trump's record on religious liberty and Catholic priorities in a statement to Fox News Digital following the archbishop's public apology. BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: MY YEAR WITH DOJ'S RELIGIOUS LIBERTY COMMISSION: WHY I SAID YES "There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it: he stopped the weaponization of the federal government against Christians, proudly defended and expanded our religious rights, pardoned pro-life activists, stopped the chemical mutilation of our nation’s children, and protected parents’ rights," she said. The meeting, which Grob said was arranged by the Heritage Foundation, was intended to address immigration enforcement, religious worker visas and other Catholic priorities. Following a 90-minute discussion with White House domestic policy staff and advisors, the bishops entered the Oval Office, where Trump presented commemorative tokens before they prayed together. Grob said the group was unaware that video was being recorded. Des Moines Bishop William Joensen also criticized the gathering's subsequent publicity in a statement published Saturday, saying the bishops never intended to endorse a political candidate or party. "None of us bishops were unaware that our meeting was on the cusp of a national election. Yet in no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," he said. "That said, in retrospect, I would have done well to be more mindful of Jesus’ admonition: ‘Behold, I am sending you like sheep in the midst of wolves; so be shrewd as serpents and simple as doves’ (Matthew 10:16). I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes." POPE LEO SLAMS THOSE WHO 'MANIPULATE RELIGION' FOR MILITARY OR POLITICAL GAIN, TRUMP RESPONDS Denver Archbishop James Golka, who led the prayer, discussed his participation in an interview with the Denver Catholic. Golka acknowledged concerns about the video's political implications but emphasized that praying for elected officials remains a longstanding Catholic practice. "I wasn’t sure what to do. On one hand, it was a great opportunity to raise important issues for the Church’s benefit," he said. "On the other hand, I knew people might be upset. Though I originally thought it would be a private meeting, I knew that it could be shared and that some might use it for political purposes. "But as I prayed about it, I thought that this is what Catholics do," he continued. "We pray for people. No matter whether we agree or disagree on anything, we always pray for our country and leaders." The controversy comes as Catholic leaders continue to disagree with the Trump administration over some of its policies, particularly immigration. The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops sued the administration in February 2025 over the suspension of refugee resettlement funding. Other prominent Catholic leaders have encouraged continued engagement with the administration. In a May interview with Fox News Digital, Bishop Robert Barron, a member of Trump's Religious Liberty Commission, cautioned against demonizing the president despite disagreements over immigration and other policies. "What I don't want from the church is a kind of demonization of the Trump administration," he said. TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Archdiocese of Milwaukee declined to comment further on the matter when reached by Fox News Digital.

articles.title: DOJ asks Washington state to set aside 400 ballots from voters it says may be noncitizens
articles.summary: The move is the Trump administration’s latest attempt to involve itself in ballot counting and certification that’s handled by state officials.
articles.body: The Trump administration targeted another state Monday by asking Washington state to sequester ballots in next week’s election that it says could be cast by noncitizens. The acting U.S. attorney in Washington, Neil Floyd, asked the Washington secretary of state to review a list of more than 400 registrants the Justice Department believes are noncitizens and sequester any ballots they cast. “We have identified over 400 non-citizens who are registered to vote and have voted in multiple elections,” Floyd said in a news release Monday. “This is only the tip of the iceberg. We will continue to investigate and identify those who are committing crimes by voting illegally.” The request came the same day the Trump administration suffered a legal setback in its push to separate thousands of ballots in California as it seeks to inject the federal government into tallying and certifying the 2026 election results. NBC News first reported last week that the Justice Department was considering bringing more requests to states with mail elections that send mail ballots to all registered voters. In a letter sent to Washington election officials that was shared with NBC News, the Justice Department gave the state 24 hours to review the list for citizenship records. Washington, which has more than 5 million voters on its voter rolls, refused to share its unredacted voter rolls with the Justice Department this year. Floyd criticized the state for that, saying Monday that it made his work more time-consuming. In an interview with conservative radio host Jason Rantz that was published Monday, Floyd said his office checked lists of permanent legal residents like green card holders against voter registration records in their search. Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs’ office is reviewing the list, spokesperson Helen Smith said in an email, though Hobbs criticized the request in a statement. “We take our responsibility to protect voter information seriously and will only respond to requests that follow due process. We saw what happened in California and don’t want Washingtonians to be harassed,” he said. “The timing of this request—one week before the General Election—is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.” Noncitizens do end up on the voter rolls sometimes, though relatively few vote, since it’s a crime with a paper trail and one that can incur serious penalties, including deportation. Newly naturalized citizens are frequently flagged as noncitizens in voting records, in large part because there is no comprehensive list of U.S. citizens. The Justice Department said last week that it believed there were 20,000 noncitizens on California’s voter rolls. It gave California 48 hours to review the administration’s list and called on it to sequester their ballots. The Trump administration later sued, asking a federal court to keep the state from counting any of those ballots. An appeals court ruled Monday against the Trump administration, saying the Justice Department had not given the lower court a chance to review the administration’s claims. Los Angeles County election officials said in a legal filing that the Justice Department’s list of suspected noncitizens appeared to come from old voting lists and included many apparent U.S. citizens whose registrations included places of birth in the U.S. The administration has sought to involve itself in ballot counting in other ways. Last week, the Trump administration — at President Donald Trump’s suggestion — sued Alaska over the candidacy of a Senate candidate with the same first and last name as the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan. The suit asks the court to block certification of the race unless the Republican senator wins re-election. Election experts told NBC News last week that the Trump administration’s various election lawsuits are on shaky ground, because nothing in federal law gives the Justice Department the authority to intervene in election certification or ballot counting.
